title: Bounded Autonomy: Between Free Will and Determinism — Angus J. McLean, Oliver

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on structuring and constraining agent systems through custom harnesses, memory, context minimization, and workflow design. Practical examples come from advertising and creative production at Oliver, while the design principles are broadly applicable across domains. The focus is on designing and building agent systems with deliberate constraints rather than deploying or monitoring them. The speaker explicitly states the talk is non-technical and accessible to beginners. A single-speaker conference presentation combining philosophical framing with practical demonstrations. summary: Angus McLean introduces 'Bounded Autonomy,' framing it as conventional wisdom for unconventional times based on his experience designing agents at Oliver, a gen AI-focused advertising agency. Oliver generates roughly 4,000 creative assets daily for over 200 brands, with significant media spend enabling performance measurement in the wild. Agents are used primarily for speed and secondarily for scale, enabling rapid iteration and localized campaign personalization. His first major advice is to slow down: despite rapid tool turnover, the core of LLMs hasn't fundamentally changed since the 1990s, and models still don't understand their inputs. He identifies key limitations — poor data efficiency, no continuous learning, inability to recognize new trends — and argues most current solutions are band-aids masking symptoms. He models the LLM as a closed box, a flexible database doing semantic math, with no expectation of emergence. While context windows have driven agentic advances, they'll never be sufficient given knowledge doubles every 12 hours. His counterintuitive approach: constrain the model deliberately. Replace internet access with high-quality documentation. Ask how little context you can use, not how much. Build your own harness and memory. The talk closes with the CV example: his complex agent app was beaten 100x by four letters — HTML. Models naturally tend toward complexity, so don't waste tokens or make extra work. He reframes AI as fundamentally translation (citing 'Attention Is All You Need'), with knowledge production as summarization, and recommends using multiple representation structures (markdown, graphs, clustering, folders, timelines) for different purposes. He stresses experimentation and play, citing hackathons as a venue for learning unavailable in his work role. Finally, invoking Adam Smith's pin factory, he notes structured workflows outperform unstructured ones, and gives a practical rule: never automate a job you cannot do yourself. He demonstrates this with a social media intelligence tool clustering 50,000 tweets into organized strategies — work he previously did manually.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Theme: Bounded Autonomy
sections.summary: McLean introduces the talk as conventional wisdom for unconventional times, exploring interactions with LLMs through the lens of bounded autonomy. Aimed at both overwhelmed beginners and experts in a rut; deliberately non-technical and non-prescriptive.

sections.title: About Oliver and GenAI in Advertising
sections.summary: Oliver is a gen AI advertising agency with 3,000 staff across 46 countries, generating ~4,000 assets daily for 200+ brands. Significant media spend enables real-world performance measurement and fast iteration feedback loops.

sections.title: Structure of an Ad Agency
sections.summary: Agencies comprise accounts (now 20%, formerly 50%), creative (20%), and strategy (20%). Creative and strategy, historically knowledge work, are now increasingly agentic — covering ideation, copywriting, content production, audience insight, and performance optimization.

sections.title: Why Agents: Speed and Scale
sections.summary: Agents are used primarily for speed (iteration, testing) and secondarily for scale (research, campaign personalization across territories). Goal: do more with less and create more effective advertising.

sections.title: Slow Down and Model Limitations
sections.summary: Advises slowing down. LLM cores haven't changed since the 1990s. Models don't understand data — poor data efficiency, no continuous learning, closed box. Recent gains are brute-force compute, not material breakthroughs.

sections.title: Band-Aid Solutions
sections.summary: Most tools and even training methods are band-aids: temporary, superficial, masking symptoms. Models should be viewed as closed boxes — flexible databases doing semantic math — with no expectation of emergence or real learning.

sections.title: Context Windows and Agent Capability
sections.summary: Recent agentic advances stem largely from increased context windows enabling longer-running tasks. But context will never be enough — world knowledge doubles every 12 hours. Challenge has shifted from getting context in to keeping noise out.

sections.title: Constraining Models with Documentation
sections.summary: Recommends replacing internet access with high-quality documentation. Models are bad at spotting promotional content and susceptible to SEO. Context is a soft constraint you can shape. Historical TF-IDF approaches contrasted with modern dynamic context assembly.

sections.title: Constraints as Creativity Driver
sections.summary: Constraints create creativity; abundance kills scrappiness. Asks how little context you can use, not how much. Draws parallels to early computing (Space War in 4,000 words, Crash Bandicoot memory optimization on PS2).

sections.title: Fundamentals: Build Your Own Harness and Memory
sections.summary: Recommends experimental use of older/smaller models, building your own harness and memory, preprocessing and archiving, understanding file systems and knowledge graphs. Cites Rosenblatt removing perceptron wires as basis for dropout — fundamentals pay off later.

sections.title: Keep It Simple: The CV/HTML Example
sections.summary: Concludes the CV anecdote: his complex agent application was beaten by four letters — HTML — a 10x to 100x improvement. Models naturally tend toward complexity, so don't waste tokens. Having god-like power doesn't mean you should use it. Build a simple version that works.

sections.title: Shorten Feedback Loops with Reality
sections.summary: When building with agents, the emphasis is on shortening feedback loops. McLean extends this to shortening feedback loops with reality itself — your ideas will collide with reality fast, so ship a simple working version first.

sections.title: AI as Translation and Knowledge as Summarization
sections.summary: AI at its core is translation, citing 'Attention Is All You Need' (originally English-to-French). The interesting extension is translating between modalities (text, images, audio, video). Knowledge production is summarization — compacting experience into useful knowledge. Structured and unstructured representations can coexist, as seen in MCP and model handoffs.

sections.title: Multiple Representation Structures
sections.summary: If data can be manipulated through a representation space, its structure is a property of the observer's needs, not the object itself. Recommends using multiple representation structures: markdown for human-readable hierarchy, graph relationships and references, clustering for large unstructured text, folders for fast retrieval, and timelines when relevant.

sections.title: Have Fun and Experiment
sections.summary: Stresses the importance of fun and experimentation. Much can only be learned through thoughtful play, not work constraints. McLean attends hackathons to experiment in ways his role doesn't allow, and the learning feeds back into his work.

sections.title: Workflows and the 'Don't Automate What You Can't Do' Rule
sections.summary: Invoking Adam Smith's pin factory, notes capitalism breaks tasks into small repeatable chunks and structured workflows outperform unstructured ones. Core rule: never automate a job unless you can do it yourself. Demonstrates with a social media intelligence tool clustering 50,000 tweets into organized strategies — work he previously did manually — now producible almost instantly for creative and strategic teams.
